title: Multiscale Experimental and Computational Methods to Characterize Hormonal and Mechanical Contributions to Pregnancy-Induced Remodeling of Skeletal Muscle
text:
Vaginal childbirth is a leading risk factor for morbid conditions that affect a quarter of U.S. women, referred to
collectively as pelvic floor disorders. Vaginal birth injury to the pelvic floor muscles is the posited link between
vaginal delivery and pelvic floor disorders, thus, this proposal will determine how pregnancy-induced remodeling
prepares these skeletal muscles for the mechanically demanding task of vaginal childbirth. Multiscale
computational and experimental methods will elucidate the hormonal and mechanical drivers of pelvic floor
muscle alterations in pregnacy that impact whole muscle active and passive mechanical function.

title: Mapping dynamic transitions across neural, behavioral, and social scales in interacting animals
text:
BBQS R34 – Zhang & Frohlich
Humans are complex systems whose health and diseases are affected by interacting elements across multiple
spatiotemporal scales. This project is highly relevant to public health as it provides a computational-
experimental framework to model behavior as a multiscale system – from neuronal activities and brain
oscillations to body movements and social relations. In the long term, it will facilitate the development of
precision medicine that integrates state-dependent interventions at all relevant scales.

title: Clonal Dynamics of the antibody response
text:
B cells produce the antibodies that help us control infections and are the primary mechanism though which
vaccines work. Although we understand well the general biology of B cells, the rules determining how the immune
system chooses what targets to make antibodies too, and how the durability of these antibodies is controlled
remain unclear. Better understanding of these rules will be essential to designing more potent vaccines against
variable pathogens such as influenza, HIV, HCV, and SARS-CoV2.

title: ADAD1 and ribosome biogenesis in the post-meiotic male germ cell
text:
Protein translation is required for normal cell function and is reliant upon proper structure and function of the
ribosome, a macromolecule composed of protein and RNA. This work will inform on the role of a male germ
cell specific RNA binding protein in ribosome biogenesis and whether some male infertility may be due to
abnormal ribosome assembly.

title: Characterization of Germline and Somatic Genetic Variants in Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis Pathogenesis
text:
Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is an inflammatory myeloid neoplasia with a median diagnosis age of 30
months and characterized by an upfront chemotherapy failure rate of 50% in patients with systemic disease
leading to disease progression associated with significant mortality, morbidity and potentially fatal progressive
neurodegeneration. Sequencing studies in small cohorts have described >50 somatic mutations in >30 genes in
non-MAPK and MAPK pathways, with activating mutations in MAPK pathway genes identified in ~80% of LCH
lesions; on the other hand, germline genetic susceptibility remains largely undefined despite evidence that
germline variants may impact susceptibility, LCH somatic mutational profiles, and adverse outcomes. This study
represents a transformative step toward understanding LCH pathogenesis by evaluating the impact of germline
variation on LCH risk and determining germline prognostic markers of LCH adverse outcomes; both of which will
highlight mechanisms for improved prevention, risk stratification, and therapeutic targets for LCH and potentially
other MAPK-driven malignancies.

title: Defining Transcriptional Regulation of CD1 Molecules in Monocyte-derived Dendritic Cells (mo-DCs)
text:
Antigen presentation is a crucial process of generating memory immune responses by activating and expanding
antigen-specific T cells. However, the field has largely focused on defining the roles and regulatory mechanisms
governing peptide-presenting molecules, known as the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). This proposal
aims to define how the expression of the understudied system of lipid antigen-presenting molecules is regulated,
which will provide novel avenues for the prevention and treatment of infectious diseases and autoimmunity.

title: Multi-disciplinary analysis of the role of PagC for outer membrane vesicle biogenesis
text:
The expression of PagC during the Salmonella infectious cycle results in a robust increase in outer membrane
vesicle biogenesis, which is a process that is essential to infectivity. However, the lack of enzymatic activity of
PagC suggests an underlying physical mechanism for induction of the membrane curvature required for outer
membrane vesicles production. Our investigations will define the physical requirements that license PagC to
induce outer membrane vesicle biogenesis, thus contributing to our understanding of a critical aspect of
Salmonella infectivity and virulence.

title: Mechanisms of Mucosal and Systemic Immunity to Vaccination and Infection with Enteric Pathogens in Children and Adults
text:
PROGRAM OVERALL – Project Narrative - CCHI
Enteric bacterial infections include different types of diarrheal illnesses caused by pathogenic Salmonella and
Shigella which afflict major populations around the world, particularly in developing nations, disproportionally
affecting children. The development of new and improved vaccines is hampered because we do not fully
understand how the human immune system operates to protect children and adults from these infections. To
address these problems, the central theme of our “Mechanisms of Mucosal and Systemic Immunity to
Vaccination and Infection with Enteric Pathogens in Children and Adults” CCHI application is to further our
understanding of the immune mechanisms that operate in both systemically and in the gut mucosal
environment, by using unique human infection and vaccination models of Salmonella and Shigella.

title: Enzyme-Powered Self-Propelled DNA Nanoparticles for Disruption and Antibiotic Delivery in Topical Biofilms
text:
We will design self-propelled urease-fueled DNA origami-based nanoparticles (DNA-SPPs) that can disrupt the
topical biofilm matrix and deliver antibiotics in most acidic regions of the biofilms for efficient bacteria killing. Aim
1 will optimize the enzymatic propulsion mechanism for directed locomotion in different urea and pH distributions,
while Aims 2 and 3 will respectively demonstrate the efficacy of DNA-SPP-mediated degradation of the biofilm
matrix and DNA-SPP-powered delivery of antibiotics to kill bacteria.

title: New York Genome Characterization Center: Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues
text:
The New York Genome Characterization Center (NYGCC) aims to contribute to the creation of a
comprehensive catalog of somatic variation in tissues from healthy individuals by applying three
state-of-the-art core sequencing assays: deep, duplex short read whole genome sequencing,
RNA sequencing, and deep long read genome sequencing. In addition, we will perform two other
assays: single cell amplification-free whole genome sequencing and targeted single cell somatic
variant genotyping of transcriptomes together with single cell gene expression. We believe the
three core assays will provide an unprecedented and comprehensive view of somatic mutations
across a variety of healthy tissues, while the two additional assays will allow us to explore the
cellular contexts and effects of the somatic variants in these tissues.

title: Developing novel CRISPR/CasX editors to generate a CCR5/null immune system
text:
HIV-1 infects cells by binding to the CD4 and the CCR5 receptors on target cells. If a cell lacks either receptor,
it is unlikely that it can be infected by most strains of HIV-1. Interestingly, some individuals have a mutation in
the gene that encodes the CCR5 receptor, and are unable to become infected with certain strains of HIV-1.
Developing methods to induce this mutation, called the CCR5-delta 32 mutation, in the stem cells of HIV-1
infected patients who do not have the mutation would potentially allow them to stop taking anti-retroviral
medications without suffering any negative effects. We propose to develop a method that replaces the normal
CCR5 gene with one carrying the CCR5-delta 32 mutation into stem cells using a newly discovered enzyme
called CasX. We will also determine how many stem cells carrying two copies of the mutation are needed for
an HIV-1 patient to stop taking anti-retroviral medications and still maintain a healthy immune system.

title: Defining the Role of Platelet ABO(H) Blood Group Antigens in Hemostasis and Thrombosis
text:
ABO blood type is an important risk factor for bleeding or thrombosis (blood clots). Little is known about
how ABO blood type impacts the function of platelets, which are critical in mediating the balance between
bleeding and clotting. The aim of this proposal is to determine which platelet proteins are decorated with the
sugars that define the different ABO blood types, and how these modifications impact platelet function.

title: Genetics, Physical Health, and Brain Perivascular Spaces during Early Adolescence
text:
Childhood and adolescence are characterized by vast structural and functional brain changes, requiring efficient
transport of metabolites to brain tissue and clearance of metabolic waste. The proposed study aims to determine
how genetic and physical health factors impact the morphology and development of brain perivascular spaces,
which are critically implicated in metabolite transport and waste clearance, in a large, longitudinal sample of U.S.
youth from 9 to 12 years-of-age. The study will fill critical gaps in our understanding of how PVS develop during
this critical period of development and will help to identify both inherited and modifiable factors that are key for
promoting brain health.

title: BOWiD: a tool for lifelong tracking C. elegans individuals using stochastically labelled landmarks
text:
Model organisms, such as the nematode C. elegans, are crucial to understand biological processes
involved in aging. There is a lack of tools to introduce directed genetic modifications easily, or to track
individual identity in C. elegans. In this project, we will develop a strategy to enable barcoding of
individual C. elegans by random labeling of cells, and thus allowing analysis of individual aging
trajectories.

title: Stanford Mendelian Genomics Research Center
text:
Discovering the genetic underpinnings of Mendelian disease to enable patient diagnosis and guide treatment is
greatly facilitated by diverse genomics assays and computational methods. To enable the next stages in
Mendelian disease diagnoses, our Mendelian Genomics Research Consortium Center will study in high detail
500 individuals and their families where current clinical genomics technologies have not achieved diagnoses.
Our Center will provide essential insights into emerging functional genomics and targeted approaches for gene
and variant discovery.

title: Shared Resource 04: Clinical-Translational Science (CTSSR)
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – CLINICAL-TRANSLATIONAL SCIENCE SHARED RESOURCE (CTSSR) The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center (OSUCCC) Clinical-Translational Science Shared Resource (CTSSR) is to foster the clinical-translational mission of the members without wet-laboratories by providing support and short-term needs for correlative science and other testable hypotheses. The CTSSR is a consultative project management and central laboratory service that was developed with a focus on investigator- initiated solid tumor clinical trials, but now supports all types of researchers, including hematological malignancy and population scientists. The CTSSR provides consultation for study design, assay choice, and laboratory and data analysis. The CTSSR assists in grant preparation, clinical trial protocol development and manuscript submission. In some cases, the CTSSR also provides the laboratory support (e.g., obtain biospecimens and then process those biospecimens when services are not available in other SR for short-term needs). The CTSSR can develop customizable portfolios of biomarker assays to provide the most innovative correlative science (e.g., emanating from Phase I and II clinical trials). The Specific Aims of the CTSSR are to: 1) provide project design and management support for clinical trial protocols, laboratory manual development, grant applications, and navigator services for studies that utilize resources available through other OSUCCC SRs and external sources; 2) provide specific laboratory services and sample processing support for clinical translational research; and, 3) develop and rigorously perform customized laboratory assays to meet the short-term needs of clinical investigators for a specific protocol, a specified time, or a specified number of patient samples. During the current funding period, the CTSSR supported 108 investigators and all five OSUCCC Research Programs. Specific future plans include enhancing interactions with other SRs; increasing support for hematologic malignancies and population science studies; expanding the cell culture facility to enable preclinical cancer cell culture studies; and providing multiplex protein profiling for biomarker discovery and validation using whole blood, plasma, serum, cells, cell/tumor extracts, and other biological fluids.

title: Cellular Imaging and Immunology Core
text: CELLULAR IMAGING AND IMMUNOLOGY CORE: PROJECT SUMMARY The Cellular Imaging and Immunology (CII) Core will be co-directed by Andrew Luster, Dennis Brown, and Shiv Pillai. This reorganized core will streamline access to state-of-the-art instrumentation, reagents, protocols, and expertise necessary for morphological, immuno-cytochemical, cell biological, and immunological studies. Central to all services are end-to-end consultations on experimental design, short- and long-term technical training, data generation, bioinformatics analysis, and data interpretation. CII Core services are organized into five major categories. Education and training activities include consultations, technical training, data generation, bioinformatics analysis, data interpretation, and the Immunology Program Series. Imaging services encompass a range of technologies, including electron microscopy, confocal or TIRF imaging, three-dimensional analysis of staining in fixed samples or in real time, and flow cytometry imaging. Immunology services include flow cytometry, cell sorting and leukocyte isolation, dendrimer-based in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence, phosphoproteomics, and histopathology. Specialized immunology services comprise next-generation sequencing to identify clonal T and B cell expansions, single-cell cloning of activated B cells, MHCII tetramers, multimers to identify, purify, and characterize antigen-specific B cells, computational approaches and CRISPR on primary immune cells, and tools to aid in the identification of causal genetic variants. Single-cell and spatial methods include single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing, high-definition spatial transcriptomics (HDST), and spatial technology platforms. The CII Core aims to advance the level of instrumentation and support for research programs of CSIBD investigators focused on basic mechanisms of disease and clinical translation in IBD and digestive disease. The specific aims of the Cellular Imaging and Immunology Core are to (1) provide access to sophisticated cellular imaging, immunological, histopathological, and single-cell and spatial transcriptomics approaches that would otherwise be prohibitive to individual researchers; (2) provide an environment for training key personnel from Center laboratories; (3) evolve to meet the needs of the CSIBD community by introducing new equipment and techniques; (4) maintain the highest level of integrity in generating, analyzing, and reporting data by focusing on quality control, rigor and reproducibility parameters in research, and data management; and (5) promote the development of junior investigators and foster collaborations by providing a connection point between investigators of varying research approaches.

title: Reconstituting human testicular germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) in vitro using iPSC-derived primordial germ cell-like cells (PGCLCs) and genetically engineered human testicular cancer cells
text:
Testicular cancer, the most common malignancy among young adult men, arise from germ cells via a
precursor lesion formed in testes of fetuses before birth. If the precursor lesion, which is known as Germ Cell
Neoplasia In Situ (GCNIS), is found in adult testes, nearly 50% of the cases will develop into fully malignant
cancers. However, due to the difficulties to obtain live GCNIS tissues or cells as well as the lack of adequate
animal models or cell culture surrogate, our knowledge on biological characteristics of GCNIS has been very
limited. Taking advantage of the recent progress in cell culture generation of human germ cells from the
induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells) and testicular cancer genetics, this R21 project will attempt to
establish cell culture and/or mouse explant models of human GCNIS, which will be useful for studying
mechanisms of testicular cancer formation as well as developing strategies to eradicate GCNIS or suppress its
progression to cancer.

title: Understanding Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 vaccine responses, in vivo and in vitro
text: We have assembled a broad and highly accomplished team to continue our investigations of Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and infection, particular focusing on subjects that are vulnerable and seeking a deeper understanding of the effects of specific antibody glycosylation and specificity, bioinformatic signatures of pan virus responses and human immune organoids and the tissues and organs they interact with.

title: AI-powered multimodal precision sensing system to track tick phenotypic responses in natural and simulated environments
text:
Protecting U.S. public health and national security from domestic and exotic tick-borne disease threats
requires ongoing, active tick surveillance at scale, combined with directed tick control. Autonomous tick
surveillance technologies offer multiple advantages over existing practices which are inefficient, costly and
require trained personnel. Here we propose innovative sensing and robotics technology to advance U.S. tick
surveillance and disease prevention capacity - an AI-powered multimodal sensing system, employing
millimeter-wave (mmWave) technology, for detection of ticks in occluded environments, mounted on an
autonomous robot trained to navigate complex, natural environments. These ground-breaking technologies will
deliver a new era in public health, distinguished by expanded tick surveillance capacity and guided, effective
tick managment, and substantial reductions in disease burden and healthcare costs.
